blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define an economic good and a free good, and use the test that tells them apart in a context.

blocks.heading: What makes a good economic or free
blocks.text: An economic good is scarce relative to wants: there is not enough for everyone who wants it at a zero price, so obtaining it requires a sacrifice, and a price is normally charged to ration it. A free good is the opposite: supply exceeds wants at a zero price, so it commands no price and no sacrifice is involved in taking it. Sunshine in the Namib is close to a free good - no one rations it and no one sells it. A 5 000-litre tanker of borehole water delivered to Windhoek is an economic good, because supplying it costs labour, fuel and pumps, and the N$180 charged is what rations the scarce delivery capacity.

blocks.heading: The test in use
blocks.text: The test that separates them is whether a price has to be paid. Apply it to two goods a beach cafe in Lisbon sees: the seawater outside its door, and the bottled seawater spray it sells to kitchens at 14 euros a bottle. The sea itself is a free good - pumping it costs almost nothing and there is more than anyone wants. The bottled spray is an economic good - labour, bottles, labels and delivery make each one scarce relative to wants, so a price is charged. Note the nuance: the same substance can be a free good in one form and an economic good in another, because scarcity is a relationship between supply and wants, not a property of the substance. Ocean water for a Norwegian fishing village would be a free good in exactly the same way.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Free goods are not the same as public goods, which topic 2.10 meets as a reason markets under-provide; and the sacrifice involved in an economic good is the opportunity cost of topic 1.3.
